You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

use clap::{value_parser, Arg, Command};

    let m = Command::new("eva")

        .arg(Arg::new("INPUT").help("Optional expression string to run eva in command mode").index(1))
        .arg(Arg::new("fix").short('f').long("fix").value_name("FIX").help("Number of decimal places in output (1 - 64)").default_value("10").value_parser(value_parser!(u64).range(1..=64)))
        .arg(Arg::new("base").short('b').long("base").value_name("RADIX").help("Radix of calculation output (1 - 36)").default_value("10").value_parser(value_parser!(u64).range(1..=36)))
        .arg(Arg::new("angle_unit").short('a').long("angle_unit").help("Angle unit").default_value("degree").value_parser(["degree", "radian", "gradian"]))
        .get_matches();
    println!("{:?} {:?} {:?} {:?}", m.get_one::<String>("INPUT"), m.get_one::<u64>("fix"), m.get_one::<u64>("base"), m.get_one::<String>("angle_unit"));
}
EOF
cargo build --release --offline 2>&1 | tail -2; ls target/release/eva"}

/// Syntax highlighting of an input line.
pub fn highlight(line: &str, settings: &Settings) -> String {
    let prev = read_highlight_ans();
    match eval_math_expression(line, prev, settings) {
        Err(_) => format!("\x1b[31m{}\x1b[0m", line),
        Ok(_) => colorize(line),
    }
}

fn read_highlight_ans() -> Option<f64> {
    let path = crate::paths::highlight_ans_path();
    let mut content = String::new();
    if let Ok(mut f) = fs::OpenOptions::new()
        .read(true)
        .write(true)
        .create(true)
        .truncate(false)
        .open(&path)
    {
        use std::io::Read;
        let _ = f.read_to_string(&mut content);
    }
    content.trim().parse::<f64>().ok()
}

fn is_op_char(c: char) -> bool {
    matches!(c, '+' | ',' | '-' | '.' | '/' | '*' | '%' | '^' | '!')
}

/// Wrap occurrences of `word` followed by one of the accepted terminators.
fn wrap_word(s: &str, word: &str, color: &str, terminator: fn(&str) -> bool) -> String {
    let mut out = String::with_capacity(s.len() + 16);
    let mut i = 0;
    let bytes = s.as_bytes();
    while i < s.len() {
        if s[i..].starts_with(word) && terminator(&s[i + word.len()..]) {
            out.push_str(color);
            out.push_str(word);
            out.push_str("\x1b[0m");
            i += word.len();
        } else {
            let ch_len = utf8_len(bytes[i]);
            out.push_str(&s[i..i + ch_len]);
            i += ch_len;
        }
    }
    out
}

fn utf8_len(b: u8) -> usize {
    if b < 0x80 {
        1
    } else if b >= 0xf0 {
        4
    } else if b >= 0xe0 {
        3
    } else if b >= 0xc0 {
        2
    } else {
        1
    }
}

fn const_terminator(rest: &str) -> bool {
    match rest.chars().next() {
        None => true,
        Some(c) => c == '\x1b' || c.is_whitespace(),
    }
}

fn func_terminator(rest: &str) -> bool {
    match rest.chars().next() {
        None => true,
        Some(c) => c == '(',
    }
}

fn colorize(line: &str) -> String {
    let mut coloured = String::with_capacity(line.len() * 2);
    for c in line.chars() {
        if is_op_char(c) {
            coloured.push_str("\x1b[35m");
            coloured.push(c);
            coloured.push_str("\x1b[0m");
        } else {
            coloured.push(c);
        }
    }
    for (name, _) in CONSTANTS {
        coloured = wrap_word(&coloured, name, "\x1b[33m", const_terminator);
    }
    // Longer names first so that e.g. "asin" wins over "sin".
    let mut names: Vec<&str> = FUNCTIONS.iter().map(|(n, _)| *n).collect();
    names.sort_by(|a, b| b.len().cmp(&a.len()));
    for name in names {
        coloured = wrap_word(&coloured, name, "\x1b[34m", func_terminator);
    }
    coloured
}

/// Evaluate a single expression given on the command line.
fn command_mode(expr: &str, settings: &Settings) {
    match eval_math_expression(expr, Some(0.0), settings) {
        Ok(ans) => {
            println!("{}", format::pprint(ans, settings.fix, settings.base));
        }
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("{}", e);
            process::exit(1);
        }
    }
}

/// Persist the latest answer (the file is overwritten in place).
fn store_answer(path: &std::path::Path, ans: f64) {
    if let Ok(mut f) = fs::OpenOptions::new().write(true).create(true).open(path) {
        let _ = writeln!(f, "{}", ans);
    }
}

/// Interactive mode.
fn repl(settings: &Settings) {
    let history_path = paths::history_path();
    let previous_ans_path = paths::previous_ans_path();

    if let Err(e) = fs::write(&previous_ans_path, "0") {
        println!("Could not write to previous_ans_path");
        println!("{:?}", e);
        process::exit(1);
    }

    let mut ed = editor::Editor::new(*settings);
    if ed.load_history(&history_path).is_err() {
        println!("No previous history.");
    }

    let mut prev_ans: Option<f64> = None;
    loop {
        match ed.readline("> ") {
            editor::ReadResult::Line(line) => {
                ed.add_history(&line);
                match eval_math_expression(&line, prev_ans, settings) {
                    Ok(ans) => {
                        prev_ans = Some(ans);
                        println!("{}", format::pprint(ans, settings.fix, settings.base));
                        store_answer(&previous_ans_path, ans);
                    }
                    Err(e) => println!("{}", e),
                }
            }
            editor::ReadResult::Interrupted => {
                println!("CTRL-C");
                break;
            }
            editor::ReadResult::Eof => break,
            editor::ReadResult::Error(msg) => {
                println!("Error: {}", msg);
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    let _ = std::io::stdout().flush();
    // Saving the history happens once, when the session ends:
    //  * nothing is written when no new entries were added;
    //  * the file is (re)created with owner-only permissions;
    //  * the "#V2" header is followed by one escaped entry per line;
    //  * at most the latest 1000 entries are kept;
    //  * lines starting with whitespace are never recorded;
    //  * consecutive duplicates are recorded only once;
    //  * it falls back to the home directory without a data directory.
    //
    // A failure to persist the history is fatal and aborts the program with
    // a panic, exactly like the tool this reimplements.
    ed.save_history_rl(&history_path.as_path()).unwrap();
}

/// Error type of the line reader, used when reporting fatal failures.
#[derive(Debug)]
#[allow(dead_code)]
enum ReadlineError {
    Io(std::io::Error),
}

impl editor::Editor {
    fn save_history_rl(&mut self, path: &std::path::Path) -> Result<(), ReadlineError> {
        self.save_history(path).map_err(ReadlineError::Io)
    }
}
